scenes.narration: Those who met Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury (Bengali: মিজানুর রহমান চৌধুরী; 19 October 1928 – 2 February 2006) was a Bengali politician, most notable for serving as Prime Minister of Bangladesh from 9 July 1986, to 27 March 1988. Chowdhury was born on 19 October 1928 in present-day Chandpur District, Bangladesh to Muhammad Hafiz Chowdhury and Mahmuda Chowdhury.

The private years of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury explain the public decades better than any speech. He went to high school in Nuria High Madrasa and went to graduate from Feni College in 1952. In 1944, Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury entered politics by joining the All Bengal Muslim Student League.

The family Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury came from matters more than the legends admit. In 1945 he was elected president of Comilla district unit of All India Muslim Students Federation. In 1946 he was made the Captain of Muslim League Volunteer Corps.

The first real success of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. He would go on to be elected the general secretary of Chandpur Muslim Chhatra League students union of Chandpur College in 1948, two years later he was elected as general secretary of Feni College students union. In 1962, he was elected to the National Assembly of Pakistan from Comilla-V.

The last chapter of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury was written long after the fame. In December 1964 he was arrested under the Public Safety Ordinance of Pakistan. He was released before the National Assembly election and went on to be elected again in the assembly from the same Constituency in 1965.

The whole life of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury reads like a single decision repeated. In 1966 he was elected to the post of organising secretary of East Pakistan Awami League and later was made the acting general secretary. On 22 June 1966 he was arrested under Defense of Pakistan Rules.

Between the birth and the legend of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury lie the years that actually decide it. In 1968 was made the convenor of the combined opposition party (COP). In the 1970 Pakistani general election he was elected to the National Assembly of Pakistan from Comilla-V for the third consecutive time.

The reputation of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury was built in the middle, not at the edges. On 30 March 1971, he went with Malek Ukil others to Agartala, Tripura, India to organize the Awami League during the War. In Kolkata he met Tajuddin Ahmad, A H M Qamaruzzaman, Syed Nazrul Islam, Muhammad Mansur Ali and other senior leaders and worked as a political motivator.

Somebody like Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. During the Liberation War of Bangladesh he worked to motivate the Bengali youths to participate in he Liberation War of Bangladesh. He frequently visited the youth camps and transit camps to motivate the Bengali youths and also met the Indian Defense Minister Jagjivan Ram to increase the number of trainee freedom fighters.

The life of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury begins far from where the story usually starts. He met Indian National Congress leader Sarat Chandra Sinha to get the support of the people of Assam in the Liberation War of Bangladesh. During his Delhi tour he participated in several seminars on the Liberation War of Bangladesh.

Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. He spend most of his time in Agartala, Shillong and Kolkata in motivating the Bengali youths and soldiers. After the independence of Bangladesh he returned to Bangladesh on 25 December.

To understand where Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury ended up, start with where Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury began. Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury was included in the Cabinet of Prime Minister Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and sworn in as a Minister on 12 January 1972. After getting the charge of Ministry of Information and Radio of Bangladesh he worked for gathering support for the party.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury ran through years nobody filmed. As a close associate of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, he was part of the founding leadership that shaped the early state institutions and communication strategy of the nascent republic. During his tenure as the Minister of Information and Radio of Bangladesh he helped the martyred radio workers family by giving them jobs in Bangladesh Betar.

Each stage of the life of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury made the next stage possible. He held the portfolio of the Minister of Information and Radio of Bangladesh till 16 March 1973. In 1973, he was elected to the 1st Jatiya Sangsad (National Parliament) representing the Awami League, and was appointed the Minister of Disaster Management and Relief, overseeing critical post-war recovery and resettlement efforts.

The people who knew Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury young describe someone already restless. During his tenure he worked in uploading 15,000 ton imported goods and relief materials from Chittagong Port. After 63 days of getting the charge of Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief he resigned from the Cabinet Council on Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's order on 17 May 1973.

What Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. After his exit from the cabinet he continued to serve as a Member of Parliament. In 1974 he led the Bangladesh Parliamentary delegation in the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association Conference.

By the time Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Later he was elected to the executive committee of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association as the representative of Asia. He also went to Sri Lanka to take part in the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association on behalf of Bangladesh.

The rise of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Following the assassination of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in 1975, the Awami League faced significant internal challenges. During the Awami League's three-day conference from 3 to 5 April 1978, Abdul Malek Ukil was elected president and Abdur Razzaq became general secretary.

Setbacks came early for Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury, and the response to them is the real story. Later disagreement was created between him and some senior leaders about BAKSAL. On 1 August 1978, he, along with Dewan Farid Gazi, formed a separate convenor committee, leading to a formal split in the party.

The legacy of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury outlived the circumstances that produced it. Subsequently, from 3 to 5 November 1978, Chowdhury's faction held its own council at Hotel Eden, electing him as president and Professor Yusuf Ali as general secretary. In the 1979 general election, under his leadership, the Awami League (Mizan) contested independently and won 2 seats in the 2nd Jatiya Sangsad.

Few lives travel as far as that of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury, and the distance is the point. His leadership during this politically volatile era signified a continued presence of democratic opposition and the original Awami League ideals. On 19 January 1985, he was included in the Cabinet of Hussain Muhammad Ershad as Senior Minister.

The childhood of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury contains the adult in small print. In 1986 he was again elected to the Jatiya Sangsad from Chandpur-4. On 9 July 1986 he was elected the Leader of the House and Prime Minister of Bangladesh.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury — in that order. Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury led the Bangladesh delegation to the 8th Summit of the Non-Aligned Movement held at Harare in Zimbabwe. In 1988 he was again elected to the Jatiya Sangsad  from Chandpur-4.

The turning point in the life of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury looked like a failure at the time. After his exit from the cabinet he was not active in Jatiya Party despite being the Vice Chairman and Presidium Member of the party. After the fall of Hussain Muhammad Ershad he was the only one who was not in jail or abroad.

Every biography of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. At this situation and on Hussain Muhammad Ershad's request he became the Acting Chairman of Jatiya Party. After becoming chairman of the party he decided to take part in the 1991 Bangladeshi general election in the banner of Jatiya Party.

The education of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury happened mostly outside any school. Under his leadership Jatiya Party began again its organizational activities from January 1991. Jatiya Party contested in 272 seats in 1991 Bangladeshi general election and won 35 seats.

What Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury wanted at the start and what Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Despite winning 35 seats in the elections Chowdhury lost his own seat to BNP's Mohammad Abdullah. In 1991 Bangladeshi general election Hussain Muhammad Ershad contested from 5 constituencies of Rangpur and went to win from all 5 constituencies.

The defining trait of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. But because constitutional obligation he chose to represent Rangpur-3 and quit the other four, triggering by-elections in them. Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury was given the nomination of Rangpur-5 and was elected from Rangpur-5 through by-election on 11 September 1991.

Those who met Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. After staying one day at Dhaka Central Jail he was taken to Bangladesh Medical University on medical grounds. Politics in Bangladesh took a decisive turn in 1994, after a by-election in Magura-2.

The private years of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury explain the public decades better than any speech. All the opposition parties including Jatiya Party demanded that the next general elections be held under a neutral caretaker government, and that provision for caretaker governments to manage elections be incorporated in the constitution. As a result, MP's of Jatiya Party and other opposition parties boycotted the parliament in 1994.

The family Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury came from matters more than the legends admit. Later all opposition MPs resigned together send their resignation to the Speaker but the speaker didn't accept it. Jatiya Party boycotted the February 1996 Bangladeshi general election which was held under the BNP led government.

The first real success of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. The election was boycotted by all major parties except the ruling BNP, who won all the seats in the parliament as a result. The new parliament, composed almost entirely of BNP members, amended the constitution to create provisions for a caretaker government (CTG).

The last chapter of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury was written long after the fame. The June 1996 Bangladeshi general election was held under a neutral caretaker government which was headed by former Chief Justice Muhammad Habibur Rahman. Chowdhury didn't contest in the election but his party won 32 seats in the elections.

The whole life of Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury reads like a single decision repeated. After the June 1996 Bangladeshi general election Awami League formed a coalition government with Jatiya Party and Anwar Hossain Manju the then General Secretary of Jatiya Party was included in the newly formed cabinet. When Awami League came to power Hussain Muhammad Ershad was released from jail on 9 January 1997.
